did_you_know.text: The phrase “They have greatly oppressed me from my youth” describes troubles and persecution that have continued since Israel’s earliest beginnings. The word “greatly” emphasizes the number of those who attacked and harmed Israel.
The words “Let Israel now say” address the people of Israel and invite them to testify for themselves about their ongoing suffering and deliverance.
The verse repeats the opening, “They have greatly oppressed me from my youth,” but adds, “yet they have not prevailed against me”: Israel’s enemies tormented it but failed to overcome it.
The image “Plowmen plowed on my back” compares Israel’s suffering to land being plowed. Plowing on the back is a powerful poetic picture of harm and torture, not a literal agricultural description.

The statement “The LORD is righteous” sets the LORD’s righteousness against the deeds of the wicked. The phrase “He has cut the cords of the wicked” portrays the LORD as severing the ropes with which the wicked sought to bind Israel.
This verse introduces the expression “those who hate Zion” for the first time in the psalm. Their fate is described as shame and retreat, in contrast to Zion’s stability.
Those who hate Zion are compared to “grass on the rooftops”—vegetation that grows on rooftops and quickly withers. The image emphasizes weak, short-lived growth that has no lasting benefit.
The grass in the image never grows enough to fill the reaper’s hand or be gathered into a sheaf. This depicts a complete failure of the harvest, not merely a poor one.

The final verse recalls the blessing passersby give to the reapers: “The blessing of the LORD be upon you,” and the reapers’ reply: “We bless you in the name of the LORD.” Here the blessing is not spoken, because the image describes a field with no real harvest.
